# Results — Study 276 (Sneaker-Resale) vs ^GSPC

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The sneaker-resale index
is a curated annual series hardcoded in [`data.py`](../sneaker_resale/data.py)
(2006–2024, base 100). S&P 500 calendar-year price returns are ^GSPC December/December
last-trading-day returns from the repo-level cache (`_cache/^GSPC_split_only.parquet`).
Match the fingerprint below to confirm you hold the same data. As-of **2026-06-17**.*

## Data stamp

| Source | Window | n observations | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| ^GSPC (S&P 500, price-only, Dec/Dec) | 2007–2024 | 18 years | `518bff365ed1` |
| Sneaker-resale index (curated, annual, appraisal-style) | 2006–2024 | 19 levels / 18 returns | hardcoded constant |

> **Price-only, not total return.** ^GSPC is a price index (no dividends); the sneaker
> "return" is pure price appreciation (sneakers pay no coupon). The two legs are
> therefore comparable on a like-for-like price basis. Adding ~1.8%/yr of S&P
> dividends would only widen the S&P's edge.

## The headline — sneakers do NOT beat stocks on return

| Metric | Sneaker-resale | ^GSPC (S&P 500) |
|---|--:|--:|
| Mean annual return | **+7.5%** | **+9.9%** |
| CAGR (2006→2024) | **+7.0%** | **+8.2%** |
| Annual volatility (reported) | 10.6% | 17.9% |
| Sharpe (rf = 0, reported) | **0.71** | 0.55 |

On *reported* numbers the sneaker index looks like a dream: lower return but far lower
volatility, so a **higher Sharpe (0.71 vs 0.55)**. That is the seductive pitch — and
it is an illusion. Two things kill it.

## Kill #1 — the outperformance is not statistically real

The mean annual **excess return (sneaker − S&P) is −2.4%/yr** — sneakers *underperform*
the index on average. The excess return is statistically indistinguishable from zero,
and certainly does not clear the |t| ≥ 2 bar in the wrong direction either:

| Test | Value |
|---|--:|
| Mean excess return | −2.4%/yr |
| One-sample t (excess vs 0) | **−0.567** |
| p-value | 0.578 |
| Newey-West HAC t (lag 1) | **−0.58** |

With only n = 18 annual observations and ~18% S&P volatility, the minimum detectable
annual excess at |t| = 2 is roughly **9%/yr** — nothing here is close. The headline
"sneakers beat stocks" claim fails on the return axis.

## Kill #2 — the high Sharpe is a stale-pricing artifact

The sneaker index is an **appraisal-style annual series**: resale prices are
aggregated and reported infrequently, so the series is heavily smoothed. Its
first-order autocorrelation is **ρ = +0.63** — a textbook stale-pricing signature
(true continuously-traded assets have annual autocorrelation near zero).

Applying a Geltner (1991) AR(1) unsmoothing to recover the economic return series:

| Metric | Reported (smoothed) | Unsmoothed (economic) |
|---|--:|--:|
| Annual volatility | 10.6% | **23.1%** |
| Sharpe (rf = 0) | 0.71 | **0.29** |

Once the smoothing is undone, the sneaker index is **more volatile than the S&P**
(23% vs 18%) and its Sharpe collapses to **0.29 — well below the S&P's 0.55**. The
"low-risk outperformance" was the index sitting on stale marks.

## Could you trade it? — frictions and the missing vehicle

There is **no investable index**: you cannot buy "the sneaker market." The only real
exposure is buying and reselling physical pairs, which carries punishing one-way costs
— marketplace seller fees (StockX/GOAT ~10–15%), authentication, shipping, storage,
and **no ability to short**. Charging a modest **3%/yr** frictional haircut takes the
sneaker mean from +7.5% to a **net +4.5%/yr**, roughly half the S&P's gross return.

A "smart" momentum overlay does not rescue it. The lagged trend rule (hold sneakers
only after an up year, one-year execution lag, net of cost) returns **+9.3%/yr** vs
**+8.2%** for buy-and-hold S&P — a +1.0pp gap on a single 18-point path with no
statistical support, i.e. overfit noise, not signal.

## The positive control

On a synthetic tape with a planted +20–30%/yr sneaker alpha, the engine's excess-return
t-stat sails past |t| = 2; with planted AR(1) smoothing and zero alpha, the reported
Sharpe inflates above the unsmoothed Sharpe exactly as on the real tape. The machinery
works — the real tape simply has no alpha and a lot of smoothing.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** Sneakers *underperform* stocks on return (−2.4%/yr excess,
  t = −0.57, HAC t = −0.58). The only "edge" is a higher reported Sharpe, which is a
  pure stale-pricing artifact: AR(1) ρ = +0.63, and unsmoothing collapses the Sharpe
  from 0.71 to 0.29 (below the S&P's 0.55). Survivorship/curation of the basket and
  the appraisal smoothing both flatter the series; neither survives scrutiny. n = 18.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** No investable index exists; the only exposure is physical
  resale with ~10–15% one-way marketplace fees, authentication, storage, and no
  shorting. Net of a conservative 3%/yr friction, sneakers return ~+4.5%/yr — roughly
  half the S&P. The hyped "alternative asset class" is unbuyable as an index and
  uneconomic as a hustle.
